Below I trace the pipelines, list the models and CV/ensemble behavior, and point out concrete bugs/problems (≥3) with file-level citations and fixes.

I. Data flow (load → preprocess → feature engineering → train → predict → submit)

I trace the two main “final submission” style pipelines present in the repo:

A) run_final_submission.py — the explicit “full submission” pipeline
- Load
  - run_final_submission.py — main()
    - train_df = pd.read_csv(BASE_DIR / 'train.csv')
    - test_df  = pd.read_csv(BASE_DIR / 'test.csv')
    (see run_final_submission.py, top of main: the two pd.read_csv calls)
- Preprocess / feature engineering (per-row numeric features)
  - run_final_submission.py — add_features(df)
    - computes avg_monthly_spend, charge_ratio, num_services, tenure_x_monthly
    (see function def add_features in run_final_submission.py)
- Target encoding (folded vs. full-train)
  - run_final_submission.py — add_te_fold(tr, va, cols, ytr, smooth=20.0)
    - used during CV to compute TE from training fold → applied to validation fold
  - run_final_submission.py — add_te_full(tr, te, cols, ytr, smooth=20.0)
    - used to compute TE from the full training set → applied to test set for final predictions
  (see both function defs add_te_fold and add_te_full in run_final_submission.py)
- Train
  - run_final_submission.py — main()
    - In CV (STEP 1) builds CatBoostClassifier(**params) and fits:
      mdl.fit(Xtr_te[fc], ytr, cat_features=ci, eval_set=(Xva_te[fc], yva), use_best_model=True)
    - In full-train (STEP 2) builds CatBoostClassifier(**params) with iterations=max(CHECKPOINTS) and fits on full data:
      mdl.fit(Xfull_te[fc], y, cat_features=ci)
    (see model.fit calls inside main of run_final_submission.py)
- Predict / Checkpoint extraction
  - run_final_submission.py — main()
    - In CV: oof[vidx] = mdl.predict_proba(Xva_te[fc])[:,1]
    - In full-train: for each checkpoint cp:
        mdl_cp = mdl.copy()
        mdl_cp.shrink(cp)
        preds = mdl_cp.predict_proba(Xtest_te[fc])[:,1]
      checkpoint_preds[cp] += preds (then averaged across seeds)
    (see the prediction code and checkpoint loop in run_final_submission.py main)
- Submit
  - run_final_submission.py — submit_to_kaggle(filepath, description)
    - uploads CSV via Kaggle API helper (calls get_kaggle_headers() from kaggle_auth)
    - called for each checkpoint file inside main
    (see function submit_to_kaggle and its calls near the end of run_final_submission.py)

B) sub_51580.py — a self-contained CV + final submission script (alternate final pipeline)
- Load
  - sub_51580.py — main(): train_df = pd.read_csv(BASE_DIR / "train.csv"), test_df = pd.read_csv(BASE_DIR / "test.csv")
- Feature engineering
  - sub_51580.py — add_features(df)
    - many extra engineered features (streaming_bundle, security_bundle, freq encodings, logs, contract_internet, tenure_bin, etc.)
- TE & group stats
  - sub_51580.py — add_te(tr, other, cols, ytr, smooth=SMOOTH) — per-fold TE
  - sub_51580.py — add_group_stats(tr, other, group_cols, num_cols)
- Train & Predict
  - sub_51580.py — get_model(seed) returns CatBoostClassifier(...) and main() runs StratifiedKFold per-seed, per-fold fits and aggregates OOF and test predictions; final submission is written with:
    sub.to_csv(BASE_DIR / "submission.csv", index=False)
  (see get_model and the training loop in sub_51580.py)

C) v2_submit_top10.py / SUBMISSION_TEMPLATE — remote submission generator
- v2_submit_top10.py builds a SUBMISSION_TEMPLATE (string) that contains:
  - add_features, add_te, add_group_stats, get_model, main (same pipeline as sub_51580 / run_final_submission), and writes submission.csv on the remote GPU host.
- v2_submit_top10.py — run_submission(...) uploads the generated script to the GPU server, executes it there, then downloads submission.csv and calls submit_to_kaggle(...)
  (see SUBMISSION_TEMPLATE and run_submission in v2_submit_top10.py)

Files / functions to inspect for pipeline steps (summary list)
- Loading:
  - run_final_submission.py: main() — pd.read_csv(...) (train/test)
  - sub_51580.py: main() — pd.read_csv(...)
  - many experiment*.py files: run_experiment() read train.csv for CV (e.g. experiment.py: run_experiment)
- Preprocess / feature engineering:
  - run_final_submission.py: add_features()
  - experiment.py / experiment_best.py / exp_* / v2_experiment_base.py: add_features()
  - sub_51580.py: add_features()
  - v2_submit_top10.py: SUBMISSION_TEMPLATE → add_features()
- Target encoding / group stats:
  - experiment.py / exp_*.py / v2_experiment_base.py: add_target_encoding(tr, va, ...)
  - run_final_submission.py: add_te_fold, add_te_full
  - sub_51580.py: add_te, add_group_stats
  - v2_pair_lr.py: target_encode_pair (nested/inner CV TE)
- Train:
  - experiment.py / exp_*.py / v2_experiment_base.py: run_experiment() uses CatBoostClassifier via get_model()
  - run_final_submission.py: main() (CatBoost training for CV and full train)
  - v2_xgb_lr.py: run_xgboost() (XGBoost)
  - v2_pair_lr.py and v2_pair_lr_ablation.py: LogisticRegression fits
  - train.py: GPT model training (big neural net) — different domain
- Predict:
  - All the above training loops call predict_proba(...) to build oof/test predictions
- Submit:
  - run_final_submission.py: submit_to_kaggle()
  - v2_submit_top10.py: submit_to_kaggle() (also uses kaggle_auth helper)
  - run_final_submission.py and v2_submit_top10.py produce CSVs in SUB_DIR (submissions/)

II. Model architectures (all distinct types used) and where they are configured

1) CatBoost (binary classification) — used everywhere for the tabular task
   - experiment.py — get_model()
     - CatBoostClassifier(
         iterations=5000,
         learning_rate=0.03,
         depth=5,
         l2_leaf_reg=5.0,
         random_strength=2.0,
         bagging_temperature=0.3,
         loss_function="Logloss",
         eval_metric="AUC",
         verbose=False,
         random_seed=SEED,
         early_stopping_rounds=300,
         task_type="GPU",
         devices="0:1",
       )
     (see experiment.py def get_model)
   - experiment_backup.py — get_model()
     - iterations=3000, learning_rate=0.03, depth=5, l2_leaf_reg=8.0, random_strength=3.0, bagging_temperature=0.0, early_stopping_rounds=200, thread_count=-1 (CPU)
     (see experiment_backup.py)
   - v2_experiment_base.py / many exp_*.py — get_model() variants
     - common variant: iterations=5000, learning_rate=0.03, depth=6, l2_leaf_reg=8.0, random_strength=2.0, early_stopping_rounds=100, task_type="GPU", devices=str(GPU_ID)
       (see v2_experiment_base.py and many exp_g*_*.py where get_model is identical)
     - some experiment files add other args:
       - exp_g0_50933.py get_model(...) includes min_data_in_leaf=5
       - exp_g1_87278.py get_model(...) includes border_count=128
       - sub_51580.py get_model(...) includes bagging_temperature=0.3, border_count=254, early_stopping_rounds=300
       (see those files' get_model definitions)
   - run_final_submission.py — CB_PARAMS dict (used for final full-train)
     - CB_PARAMS = dict(
         learning_rate=0.03,
         depth=5,
         l2_leaf_reg=5.0,
         random_strength=2.0,
         bagging_temperature=0.8,
         min_data_in_leaf=50,
         loss_function='Logloss',
         eval_metric='AUC',
         verbose=False,
         task_type='GPU',
         devices='0:1',
       )
     (see run_final_submission.py CB_PARAMS near top)

2) XGBoost
   - v2_xgb_lr.py — run_xgboost() builds an XGBClassifier:
     - xgb.XGBClassifier(
         n_estimators=5000,
         learning_rate=0.03,
         max_depth=6,
         reg_lambda=8.0,
         subsample=0.8,
         colsample_bytree=0.8,
         min_child_weight=5,
         objective="binary:logistic",
         eval_metric="auc",
         tree_method="hist",
         device="cuda",
         random_state=seed,
         verbosity=0,
         early_stopping_rounds=100,
       )
     (see v2_xgb_lr.py run_xgboost model definition)

3) Logistic Regression (scikit-learn)
   - v2_pair_lr.py — meta-model after pair TE → LogisticRegression(
         penalty="l2", C=0.5, max_iter=4000, tol=1e-4, solver="lbfgs", n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED)
     (see v2_pair_lr.py when creating lr)
   - v2_xgb_lr.py — run_logistic_regression uses LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000, solver="lbfgs", random_state=seed, n_jobs=-1)
     (see v2_xgb_lr.py run_logistic_regression)

4) Neural transformer (GPT) — large language model training code
   - train.py defines:
     - GPTConfig dataclass (defaults: sequence_len=2048, vocab_size=32768, n_layer=12, n_head=6, n_kv_head=6, n_embd=768, window_pattern="SSSL")
     - class GPT(nn.Module) builds transformer with n_layer, n_head, n_kv_head, n_embd
     - model built later via build_model_config(depth) where DEPTH is set at top: DEPTH = 8 (so actual n_layer = 8 in default run)
     - other hyperparameters at top: ASPECT_RATIO=64, HEAD_DIM=128 → these determine model_dim and num heads; optimizer: MuonAdamW, schedule constants, TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE, device batch size, etc.
     (see train.py: GPTConfig, GPT class and top-level hyperparameters)

Those are the distinct model families used: CatBoost (main tabular models), XGBoost (alternate), scikit-learn LogisticRegression (meta / simple models), and a full neural transformer (train.py) used for a different part of the codebase.

III. Cross-validation strategy and leakage review

Common pattern across most tabular scripts
- StratifiedKFold is used everywhere to preserve class balance:
  - experiment.py (and many exp_*.py): skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED) then loop over skf.split(X, y) and fit per-fold (see experiment.py run_experiment).
  - exp_combo_7920.py and many exp_*.py do an outer seed ensemble: seeds = [42,52,62]; for each seed they do StratifiedKFold(random_state=seed) and collect oof per-seed, then average across seeds:
    - all_oof = np.zeros((len(seeds), len(X))) ; ensemble_oof = all_oof.mean(axis=0)
    (see exp_combo_7920.py run_experiment: the seeds loop and all_oof mean)
- run_final_submission.py uses N_SEEDS = 7 and N_FOLDS = 5:
  - In STEP 1 it runs CV per seed to choose iteration (skf = StratifiedKFold(..., random_state=seed)), collects best iteration per fold and oof predictions.
  - In STEP 2 it trains on full data per seed and aggregates test predictions across seeds.
  (see run_final_submission.py main)

Nested CV for Target Encoding in pair-logit pipeline
- v2_pair_lr.py (and v2_pair_lr_ablation.py) use nested CV for target encoding:
  - Outer CV: StratifiedKFold(n_splits=N_OUTER)
  - Inner CV for target encoding within each outer training fold: inner_kf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=N_INNER_TE, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED + 999) inside target_encode_pair() (this produces leak-free OOF TE for the training fold)
  - For validation and test, mapping is computed on the full outer training fold (df_full) and applied to val/test
  (see v2_pair_lr.py: target_encode_pair and where inner_kf is defined)

Potential leakage / risks (explicit)
1) Label-encoding using train+test (possible distribution leakage)
   - v2_pair_lr.py — label encoding block at start of main():
     - For each categorical column:
       tr_s = train_enc[c].astype(str).fillna("__MISSING__")
       te_s = test_enc[c].astype(str).fillna("__MISSING__")
       all_vals = pd.concat([tr_s, te_s], axis=0)
       uniq = sorted(all_vals.unique())
       mapping = {v:i for i, v in enumerate(uniq)}
       train_enc[c] = tr_s.map(mapping).astype(np.int32)
       test_enc[c]  = te_s.map(mapping).astype(np.int32)
     (see v2_pair_lr.py — lines where all_vals = pd.concat([tr_s, te_s]) is used)
   - Issue: concatenating train+test to build label encoder leaks information about test-set categories into the mapping (not target labels, but distributional information). This is often accepted for final training but is a potential leakage risk when used during CV experiments. Safer approach: fit mapping on train only and map test with .get(..., unseen_value).
2) Frequency encoding computed globally (pre-split) in experiment variants
   - run_batch.py experiment "feat_freq_encoding" constructs frequency features inside add_features on the entire DataFrame (df[f"{c}_freq"] = df[c].map(df[c].value_counts(normalize=True))). Because add_features is invoked before CV splitting (most experiment scripts call add_features(train_df.drop(columns=[TARGET]))), these frequency features are computed globally and therefore validation rows see features aggregated over the whole dataset. This is a potential leakage/overfitting source (see run_batch.py experiments list → "feat_freq_encoding" patch).
   - Safer approach: compute frequency maps inside each CV fold (from Xtr) and then map to Xva (and test) — same approach used for target-encoding/group-stats functions in other files.
3) Target encoding usage is generally per-fold (safe) in most scripts
   - Most experiment files call add_target_encoding(Xtr, Xva, CAT_COLS, ytr) inside the fold loop (safe). The pair-TE pipeline uses nested inner CV to get leak-free OOF for training (also safe).
   - check: experiment.py and v2_experiment_base.py call add_target_encoding inside the fold loop (see those files).

IV. Ensemble methods (how predictions are combined)

I list the ensemble / blending strategies used in this codebase and cite code:

1) Seed averaging (multi-seed ensemble)
   - Pattern: train using multiple random seeds (e.g. seeds = [42, 52, 62] or N_SEEDS = 7), collect OOF/test predictions per seed and average final probabilities across seeds.
   - Example: exp_combo_7920.py (and many exp_* / v2_*.py)
     - all_oof = np.zeros((len(seeds), len(X))); each seed fills oof → all_oof[si] = oof ; ensemble_oof = all_oof.mean(axis=0)
     (see exp_combo_7920.py run_experiment)
   - run_final_submission.py:
     - For final full-train predictions: checkpoint_preds[cp] accumulates preds from each seed; after loop they divide by N_SEEDS:
       checkpoint_preds[cp] /= N_SEEDS
     (see checkpoint accumulation and averaging lines in run_final_submission.py)
2) Fold averaging (within-seed CV ensembling)
   - During CV, test predictions are collected by averaging predictions from each fold (typical K-fold ensembling):
     - sub_51580.py inside per-seed loop: test_preds += model.predict_proba(Xte_fold[fc])[:, 1] / N_FOLDS
     - After finishing all folds for a seed, all_test[si] = test_preds ; then final ensemble average across seeds is all_test.mean(axis=0)
     (see sub_51580.py training loop and test_preds accumulation)
3) Checkpoint ensembles (run_final_submission.py)
   - run_final_submission.py constructs multiple submissions for different iteration checkpoints CHECKPOINTS = [500,1000,...,5000]; for each checkpoint it collects seed-average predictions and writes separate CSVs per checkpoint (no stacking between checkpoints; each checkpoint is a separate submission file).
   - Implementation: for each seed train full model with max iterations, then for cp in CHECKPOINTS: mdl_cp = mdl.copy(); mdl_cp.shrink(cp); preds = mdl_cp.predict_proba(...); checkpoint_preds[cp] += preds ; after seeds: checkpoint_preds[cp] /= N_SEEDS → write CSV per cp.
   (see the checkpoint loop in run_final_submission.py)
4) Stacking/meta model (pair-TE → Logit³ → LogisticRegression)
   - v2_pair_lr.py:
     - It target-encodes feature pairs (pair TE) with inner CV to produce OOF TE values for training folds, then for each pair applies a logit transform and creates polynomial features z, z^2, z^3, concatenates them, StandardScaler, then fits a single LogisticRegression on top of those transformed features.
     - Final predictions are obtained by averaging outer folds for the test set (pred_meta accumulated / N_OUTER).
     (see v2_pair_lr.py: target_encode_pair, make_logit3, StandardScaler + LogisticRegression)
5) Simple averaging of model outputs (no weighted blending)
   - Throughout, averaging is simple arithmetic mean of predicted probabilities (no stacking of different model types except when logistic regression is used as a meta-model for the pair-TE approach).

V. Bug hunt — explicit issues, file references, why they are problems and fixes (≥3)

I list concrete problems I found (each includes file + code pointer + suggested fix).

Bug 1 — Missing/undefined kaggle_auth helper (submit will fail)
- Files / lines:
  - run_final_submission.py — submit_to_kaggle() (function body starts "from kaggle_auth import get_kaggle_headers")
    - See submit_to_kaggle definition in run_final_submission.py (function uses: from kaggle_auth import get_kaggle_headers)
  - v2_submit_top10.py — at file top: from kaggle_auth import get_kaggle_headers
- Problem: There is no kaggle_auth.py in this repository. The submit_to_kaggle functions call get_kaggle_headers() from kaggle_auth which will ImportError at runtime unless that external helper exists on the system. Submission functions will fail.
- Fix:
  - Provide a kaggle_auth.py implementation that returns appropriate Authorization headers (or read KAGGLE_USERNAME/KAGGLE_KEY from environment and build headers); or
  - Replace custom code with the official kaggle API (kaggle) or the REST API via a documented token; e.g., use kaggle CLI: subprocess.run(["kaggle", "competitions", "submit", "-c", COMP, "-f", filepath, "-m", description]) or use kaggle.api.KaggleApi to manage uploads. This is safer and standard.

Bug 2 — Incorrect / inconsistent XGBoost GPU parameters
- File / lines:
  - v2_xgb_lr.py — run_xgboost() model instantiation:
    - xgb.XGBClassifier(..., tree_method="hist", device="cuda", ...)
- Problem:
  - tree_method="hist" is the CPU histogram implementation; for GPU use you must set tree_method="gpu_hist" and (in older versions) specify gpu_id. The parameter device="cuda" is not a standard XGBClassifier parameter and is likely ignored or will error depending on xgboost version. This suggests either intended GPU training is misconfigured or the code will fall back to CPU unexpectedly.
- Fix:
  - For GPU training, set tree_method="gpu_hist" and optionally gpu_id=0 (or appropriate), and remove the invalid device="cuda" kwarg. Example:
      xgb.XGBClassifier(..., tree_method="gpu_hist", gpu_id=0, predictor="gpu_predictor", ...)
  - Alternatively, remove GPU arguments to ensure reproducible CPU runs if GPU not available.

Bug 3 — Label encoding fit on train+test (possible distribution leak)
- File / lines:
  - v2_pair_lr.py — label-encoding block near top of main():
    - all_vals = pd.concat([tr_s, te_s], axis=0)
    - uniq = sorted(all_vals.unique())
    - mapping = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(uniq)}
    - train_enc[c] = tr_s.map(mapping)
    - test_enc[c] = te_s.map(mapping)
- Problem:
  - Building the mapping from concatenated train+test leaks test-set category information into the encoder. While no target values leak, this gives the training process knowledge of which categories exist in the test set and their ordinal ordering — not a strict label leak but can bias preprocessing and is generally considered poor practice during model selection/CV.
- Fix:
  - Fit label mapping on train only: mapping = {v:i for i,v in enumerate(sorted(tr_s.unique()))}, map train and map test with .map(mapping).fillna(unseen_value) (e.g., -1) or add an "UNSEEN" category. If the goal is to keep consistent mapping for final submission, you can after CV build a final mapping on train+test only for the final full fit (but do not use train+test mapping during CV).

Bug 4 — Frequency encoding computed globally before CV (leak risk)
- File / lines:
  - run_batch.py — experiments list includes "feat_freq_encoding" patch:
    - Replacement adds:
      for c in ["Contract", "InternetService", "PaymentMethod"]:
          df[f"{c}_freq"] = df[c].map(df[c].value_counts(normalize=True)).astype(np.float32)
    - This modifies add_features so the frequency is computed from the entire dataset before CV.
- Problem:
  - Computing aggregated statistics (even if not target) on the entire dataset before splitting can leak information about the validation rows into features used for training, especially for small sample counts or in combination with other features/regularization it can artificially boost CV metrics.
- Fix:
  - Compute frequency encoding per-fold: inside the CV loop, build freq map from Xtr: freq_map = Xtr[c].value_counts(normalize=True); then map to Xva (and to the test set using the training-fold map). The project already does this pattern for target-encoding and group stats (see add_target_encoding/add_group_stats which take tr & va), so move frequency encoding to be folded in the same way.

Bug 5 — Potential invalid use of CatBoost model methods for checkpoint extraction
- File / lines:
  - run_final_submission.py — in the checkpoint extraction loop:
    - mdl_cp = mdl.copy()
    - mdl_cp.shrink(cp)
    - preds = mdl_cp.predict_proba(Xtest_te[fc])[:,1]
- Problem:
  - The code assumes CatBoost Python model supports copy() and shrink() to obtain a model truncated at a given number of trees. Depending on CatBoost version, copy() and shrink() may not exist or shrink() may not behave as expected. If shrink() is not available, this will raise AttributeError at runtime.
- Fix:
  - Use the CatBoost API-supported approach to get predictions for first N trees; CatBoost’s predict_proba supports ntree_end / ntree_start arguments (e.g., predict_proba(data, ntree_end=cp)). Use that to get predictions per checkpoint without relying on copy()/shrink().
    - Example fix:
        preds = mdl.predict_proba(Xtest_te[fc], ntree_end=cp)[:,1]
    - Confirm CatBoost version and its API; test locally. Alternatively train separate models saved at intervals, or call mdl.save_model(ntree_end=cp) if supported.

(Those five items include 3+ serious issues: missing kaggle_auth, XGBoost GPU param misuse, label-encoding leakage, global frequency leakage, and questionable CatBoost shrink usage.)
